ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
A large square is divided into 4 equal-sized smaller squares. All the smaller squares are either shaded or unshaded. How many different ways are there to colour the large square? (Two colourings are considered to be the same if one can be rotated to look exactly like the other, as in the example shown.)

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached figure shows a large square composed of two 2×2 small grids, with an equals sign in the middle. In the 2×2 grid on the left, only the upper-left small square is shaded black; in the 2×2 grid on the right, only the lower-right small square is shaded black. This shows that if two patterns can completely coincide through rotation, they are counted as the same coloring method. Reasoning: The large square has a total of 4 small squares, and each small square has only two states, shaded or unshaded. Classify by the number of small squares shaded black: when 0 are shaded black, there is only 1 kind; when 4 are shaded black, there is only 1 kind; when 1 is shaded black, any corner can become any other corner through rotation, so there is only 1 kind; when 3 are shaded black, it is equivalent to having only 1 unshaded, and similarly there is only 1 kind; when 2 are shaded black, there are 2 different types: the two shaded black squares are adjacent, or the two shaded black squares are opposite on a diagonal. The total number is 1+1+1+1+2=6.

method.method_draft: First describe the image: it presents two 2-by-2 colourings with one shaded square each and marks them equal, showing that the rotation group of the square should be used. From the text, there are 4 positions, each independently shaded or unshaded before identifying rotations, so there are 2^4=16 raw colourings. Apply Burnside's lemma for the 4 rotations of the square. The identity rotation fixes all 16 colourings. A 90-degree rotation fixes only colourings where all four cells have the same colour, so 2. A 180-degree rotation fixes colourings where opposite cells match, giving 2^2=4. A 270-degree rotation is like 90 degrees, so 2. The number of distinct rotational equivalence classes is the average: (16+2+4+2)/4=6.
